questions.question: Design a search autocomplete/typeahead feature for a 10 million product catalog.
questions.title: Design Search Autocomplete for a Product Catalog
questions.direct_answer: Pre-compute autocomplete suggestions using a trie or sorted set in Redis. For real-time search, use Elasticsearch with prefix queries and edge n-gram tokenization. Cache top suggestions per prefix. Update suggestions asynchronously from search analytics.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of prefix search data structures, caching, and search relevance
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using LIKE 'query%' on a relational database — doesn't scale past 100k products
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain edge n-gram tokenization for Elasticsearch prefix queries and how to weight suggestions by popularity

sections.title: Why LIKE 'query%' Breaks at 100K Products
sections.content:
Autocomplete must respond in under **100ms** — users expect suggestions to appear as they type, and anything slower feels laggy. With a 10-million-product catalog, a naive SQL query (`SELECT name FROM products WHERE name LIKE 'lap%' ORDER BY popularity LIMIT 10`) scans a B-tree index for prefix matches. This works fine at 10,000 products. At 10 million, with concurrent users typing, the database buckles — each keystroke generates a query, and at 1,000 concurrent users typing at 3 characters/second, that's **3,000 queries/second** of full prefix scans.

The solution is a **purpose-built search index** — Elasticsearch with edge n-gram tokenization, or a Trie-based in-memory data structure. Both are optimized for prefix lookups: Elasticsearch pre-indexes every prefix at write time so reads are O(1) index lookups, while a Trie traverses the prefix path in O(k) where k is the query length.

The harder problem isn't just finding matches — it's **ranking** them. "lap" should return "laptop" before "lapel pin" because laptops are searched more frequently. Ranking combines prefix matching with popularity signals, recency, and personalization.

sections.title: Edge N-gram Indexing: How Elasticsearch Makes Prefix Search Fast
Ranking: Why the Most Popular Result Must Come First
sections.content:
Returning all products matching "lap" alphabetically is useless. The user almost certainly wants "laptop" — the most popular match. Ranking combines multiple signals, weighted by importance.

**Popularity score** (search frequency, purchase count) is the primary signal. Store a popularity counter per product, updated daily from analytics. Elasticsearch's `function_score` query multiplies the text match score by the popularity weight.

**Recency** matters for trending products. A product launched this week with moderate search volume should rank above a discontinued product with historical popularity. Apply a decay function that reduces the score of older products.

**Personalization** is the advanced tier. If the user previously browsed electronics, boost electronic products in autocomplete results. This requires a user profile service and adds latency — only worthwhile at scale.

The practical implementation scores results as `text_match * log(popularity + 1) * recency_decay`. The `log` prevents extremely popular products from completely dominating — a product with 10x the popularity should rank higher, but not 10x higher. Recency decay uses a half-life of 30 days: products older than 30 days get half the recency boost.

Caching adds another layer — the top 1,000 most common queries are cached in Redis with a 5-minute TTL. Since autocomplete queries follow a power-law distribution (a few prefixes account for most traffic), this cache serves 60–80% of requests without hitting Elasticsearch.

sections.title: Client-Side Optimization: Debounce, Minimum Length, and Cancellation
sections.content:
The autocomplete experience is as much about **what you don't send** as what you do. Three client-side optimizations reduce server load by 70–80%.

**Debouncing** delays the API call until the user pauses typing — typically 200–300ms. Without debounce, typing "laptop" fires 6 requests ("l", "la", "lap", "lapt", "lapto", "laptop"). With 300ms debounce, it fires 1 request ("laptop"). This single optimization eliminates the majority of autocomplete traffic.

**Minimum query length** of 2–3 characters prevents uselessly broad queries. A search for "l" matches millions of products — the results are meaningless and the query is expensive. Only send requests after 2+ characters.

**Request cancellation** aborts in-flight requests when the user types another character. If the user types "la" and then "p" before the "la" response arrives, cancel the "la" request — the results are already stale. In JavaScript, this uses `AbortController`; in mobile, cancel the Retrofit/URLSession request.

The combination of these three — debounce 300ms + min length 2 + cancellation — reduces autocomplete API calls by roughly 80% compared to sending a request on every keystroke. This is often the difference between needing 5 Elasticsearch nodes and needing 1.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Trie structure gives O(L) lookup where L = query length** — each node in the trie represents one character.
- **Pre-compute top-N suggestions per prefix** — at query time you want to read the answer, not compute it.
- **Prefix cache in Redis with serialized suggestion lists** — key is the lowercase prefix, value is a serialized list of {suggestion, score}.
- **Client-side debounce (150–200ms) reduces QPS by 3–5×** — users type faster than 100ms/character.
- **Personalization layer adds recency bias** — blend global popularity score with user's own query history using weighted sum.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Autocomplete must respond in under 100 milliseconds — users expect suggestions to appear as they type, and any perceived lag causes users to stop using it. The system at 10 million users generates roughly 50K–100K prefix queries per second at peak typing speed. This latency and throughput requirement drives every design decision.

**The trie data structure and precomputation:**
- A trie gives O(L) lookup time where L is the query length — O(1) per character regardless of total dictionary size; each node represents one character and points to children
- But traversing the trie at query time to find and rank all matches is too slow at this scale; instead, pre-compute the top-N suggestions for each prefix offline
- The analytics pipeline counts query frequencies hourly; the top 5 suggestions per prefix are written to Redis with the prefix as the key and a serialized ranked list as the value; query time is a single Redis GET

**Serving the suggestions:**
- A single Redis GET per prefix lookup takes ~1ms round-trip; for a 5-character query, you serve 5 Redis lookups (one per prefix length) in parallel or just the current prefix
- Client-side debounce (150–200ms) is the highest-leverage optimization: users type faster than 100ms per character, so debouncing reduces backend QPS by 3–5× without any perceptible latency increase
- CDN edge caching for common prefixes: "ja", "py", "co" — the top 1,000 most common prefixes handle 80% of queries; cache at the CDN edge for zero-latency serving

**Personalization and freshness:**
- Blend global popularity score with user's own recent query history using a weighted sum; prevents irrelevant suggestions for users with different vocabularies; fall back to global for new users
- Refresh the Redis precomputed suggestions every 15 minutes from the analytics pipeline; trending topics appear in autocomplete within 15 minutes of spiking

I recommend precomputed Redis serving with client-side debouncing as the core architecture, CDN caching for top common prefixes, and an offline analytics pipeline refreshing suggestions every 15 minutes.

A search for "lap" is a simple term lookup — no prefix scanning, no wildcard matching
The index configuration specifies the minimum and maximum n-gram lengths
